messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thanh is a 35-year-old Vietnamese American UX designer who lives with his wife in a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest. He was referred for psychological assessment following a period of severe functional decline, presenting with a PCL-5 score of 73. His difficulties trace back to a hospitalization eighteen months ago, when what he had dismissed as persistent fatigue and intermittent chest tightness was diagnosed as a serious cardiac arrhythmia requiring emergency intervention. He spent eleven days in the ICU, during which his heart stopped twice and was restarted with a defibrillator. He remembers the overhead lights, the sound of the monitor alarm, and the particular quality of silence that followed the second episode — a silence he has described as feeling like the world pausing to decide whether to continue without him.

In the weeks after discharge, Thanh told himself he had simply survived something difficult and should move forward. He returned to work designing digital interfaces, a job that had always rewarded his precision and control. But the recovery that was supposed to follow did not arrive. Instead, something subtler and more corrosive took hold. He had come to believe, in a way he could not fully articulate, that there was something fundamentally wrong with him — not just medically, but as a person. He found himself interpreting the illness as evidence of an inner defectiveness, a weakness of constitution that others without his history did not carry. He felt, in his own words, "dead inside," as though the emotional range that had once made him an engaged husband and a creative professional had been quietly evacuated. These appraisals — that he was broken, that he was weak — drove him to avoid anything that might confirm them. He stopped attending routine follow-up appointments, reasoning that if he did not look, he could not be told something was wrong again. He declined a gym membership his wife suggested, steering away from any situation that might place his body under physical stress and thereby prove, once more, that it could not be trusted.

Yet this avoidance did not bring relief. Because Thanh was no longer receiving medical reassurance, and because he had severed the ordinary feedback loops that might have told him his body was functioning adequately, his sense of threat expanded to fill the space. His body felt constantly tense, poised at the edge of reaction. When a project at work ran past its deadline — a common enough occurrence in his field — he experienced a cold certainty that the delay signified catastrophe, that something was going wrong that no one was telling him about. He had lost the capacity to accept reassurance: when his cardiologist's office called to reschedule a check-in, his wife gently told him it was routine, and he found it genuinely impossible to believe her. The elevated threat perception, in turn, deepened his conviction that he was fragile and defective — a man whose nervous system could not distinguish a missed Slack notification from mortal danger must surely be fundamentally impaired.

This heightened state of alarm then fed back into his avoidance. The more dangerous the world felt, the more Thanh retreated from anything that resembled a medical context. He began taking alternate routes to avoid the hospital district on his commute. When a colleague mentioned having been in an ambulance the previous year, Thanh excused himself from the conversation. At work, he has begun declining in-person client meetings that require him to travel, offering technical reasons that obscure the real one: that unfamiliar environments feel impossible to monitor for threat. His wife has noticed the withdrawal, and the distance between them has grown in proportion to what he cannot explain to her.

The emotional numbness Thanh reports — that sense of being dead inside — sits alongside these dynamics without appearing to drive them directly. He notices it most in the evenings, when he and his wife used to talk, and finds he has little to offer.

What finally brought Thanh to seek help was a moment at his desk three weeks ago when his heart skipped a beat — a benign palpitation — and he spent four hours certain he was dying, unable to work, unable to call anyone. What he most fears is that this is simply who he is now. What he most hopes is that it isn't.
